claims.title: Order-submission flooding can exhaust the storefront API and propagate load into order capture
claims.description: An attacker with a valid shopper session can repeatedly submit orders over `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` from the public-internet side of its boundary crossing. Each accepted submission causes `process:storefront-api` to forward the order over `flow:process:storefront-api>process:order-service>submit-order`, so attacker traffic consumes public API request capacity and drives work into `process:order-service` rather than ending at the edge. If request-rate, concurrency, input-size, and downstream timeout limits are not present, the attacker spends repeated ordinary requests while API workers and order-capture capacity are consumed; legitimate shoppers cannot place orders. Second-order, saturation of `process:order-service` delays its order persistence to `store:orders-db` and receipt creation to `store:receipt-archive`.

quotes.text: It is the only thing we expose to the internet.
When a shopper submits an order the storefront API calls the order service over gRPC.

severity.justification: Likelihood is medium: `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order` crosses from `boundary:public-internet`, but the stated session-cookie authentication requires an attacker to obtain or create a shopper session. Impact is medium: flooding `process:storefront-api` disrupts shopper ordering and propagates over the crossing into `process:order-service`; the model shows the resulting persistence and receipt paths but does not establish an irreversible outage.

mitigations.summary: Apply identity-aware request and work limits to order submission
mitigations.detail: Set per-session, per-account, and per-source rate and concurrency limits on `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`, with hard request-size bounds before order processing.

Use bounded queues or concurrency limits between `process:storefront-api` and `process:order-service`, with short timeouts and load shedding so public bursts cannot consume all order-service capacity.

claims.title: Unverified settlement-webhook authentication may permit anonymous flooding of the shared storefront API
claims.description: `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` crosses from `boundary:public-internet` into the only internet-exposed process, but both its authentication and origin verification are unverified. If those unknowns resolve to absent or ineffective webhook authentication, an unauthenticated internet attacker can cheaply POST settlement-shaped requests to `process:storefront-api` and exhaust its request workers, connection capacity, or downstream processing budget. The same shared API also receives shopper order traffic on `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`; therefore a flood on the webhook route can deny legitimate order placement even though the attacker never needs a shopper session. This is conditional on the unresolved authentication and origin-verification facts, not an assertion that the processor callback is currently unsigned.

quotes.text: I would have to check how that callback is authenticated.
After they settle a payment they POST a webhook back to the storefront API to tell us the order is paid.

severity.justification: Likelihood is high conditional on `unknown:flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook:authentication` and the unverified origin-verification assertion: the flow crosses from `boundary:public-internet`, so no credential prerequisite is established if the unknown resolves unfavorably. Impact is medium because `process:storefront-api` is shared by the webhook and the shopper order flow, so its saturation interrupts ordering, while the modeled availability loss is recoverable.

mitigations.summary: Authenticate and bound webhook traffic before processing
mitigations.detail: Verify a processor-specific signature and replay window on `flow:entity:card-processor>process:storefront-api>settlement-webhook` before settlement handling; impose strict body-size, per-source rate, and concurrent-request limits.

mitigations.summary: Isolate webhook capacity from shopper ordering
mitigations.detail: Separate or bulkhead webhook handling from shopper-facing capacity in `process:storefront-api`, and use bounded asynchronous processing so callback bursts cannot starve `flow:entity:shopper>process:storefront-api>place-order`.
